Feuerbach

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move the corners of a triangle and watch a special circle touch four other circles.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and press the arrow keys. Tick a box to show or hide its guides, and press Reset to put the triangle back.
Look for the math

A triangle carries a circle through its side midpoints and the feet of its heights. Surprising as it sounds, that same circle always touches the circle inside the triangle and each of the three circles outside it. Drag the corners to see how far you can stretch the triangle before this stops looking true.

A circle through nine points

The midpoints of AB, BC and CA lie on one circle: the nine-point circle. It also passes through the feet of the three heights and the midpoints from each corner to the orthocenter. Its centre N is halfway between the triangle's circumcentre O and the orthocenter H, and its radius is R/2, where R is the circumradius. The applet builds it as the circumcircle of the three side midpoints, averaging the three distances from its centre to them; the logic test checks that this is R/2 on every triangle in its sample.

Four circles that touch

The incircle has centre I and radius r; each excircle has centre I_a and radius r_a. The applet finds those centres from angle bisectors and takes each radius as the mean of the distances to the three side lines. Feuerbach's discovery is that IN = R/2 − r while IN_a = R/2 + r_a. In other words the incircle sits inside the nine-point circle and touches it internally, while each excircle lies outside and touches it externally. The incircle's Feuerbach point is marked F. These equalities hold throughout the test's hundreds of triangles. There is one edge case the page does not mention: for an equilateral triangle r = R/2 and N = I, so the two circles coincide and there is no single F.

What the neighbouring pages add

This applet draws only the triangle, the four circles and their four dots. The nearby Incidence page goes further: it joins each corner to the touch point on the opposite excircle and asks whether those three lines meet, and whether N, that point, I and F lie on one line (its text calls four points "concurrent"). The Proof page establishes the tangency by inversion in a circle, rather than by the distances Feuerbach computed. The Four Triangles, One Circle page puts the orthocenter to work: ABC and the three triangles made with H share one nine-point circle, tangent in general to sixteen circles. None of those extra constructions belongs to this applet; the live droodle page now keeps only the text, while a 2006 archived copy still embeds CODE="Feurebach" twice.

Make the triangle almost equilateral and watch I and N merge: the single Feuerbach point becomes every point of a shared circle. Then pull one corner far away and see which excircle leaves the screen first.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
